document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman is 2 d post hip fracture repair. Nurses report that she was lucid at breakfast but by evening is drowsy, rambling, and unable to sustain attention through a sentence; overnight she pulled at her IV. Her daughter states her memory and independence were normal before admission. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Delirium is an acute, potentially reversible disturbance in cognition, attention, or level of consciousness. Using the Confusion Assessment Method, delirium is likely when there is acute onset with a fluctuating course plus inattention, together with either disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness. Delirium occurs in about 50% of patients after high-risk procedures such as hip fracture repair, and this woman fluctuated within a day with inattention, disorganized speech, and drowsiness on a normal cognitive baseline.

optionExplanations.b: Dementia develops gradually over months to years with a normal level of consciousness and attention intact initially; her baseline was normal 2 d ago.
optionExplanations.c: Vascular dementia also follows a gradual or step-wise course over months to years, not hours, and does not fluctuate with a depressed level of consciousness.
optionExplanations.d: Depression is subacute over weeks to months with a normal level of consciousness, intact orientation, and reduced concentration rather than fluctuating inattention.
optionExplanations.e: Normal aging causes only mild changes in working memory and processing speed, not acute fluctuating confusion.

questions.question: An 80-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment is admitted to a general medical ward with pneumonia. His glasses and hearing aids were left at home, he is on continuous IV fluids with a urinary catheter, and he has been kept in bed. The team wants to reduce his risk of developing delirium. Which of the following is the most appropriate strategy?

options.text: Scheduled nightly lorazepam to consolidate sleep
A multicomponent non-pharmacologic program (reorientation, cognitive stimulation, sleep hygiene, early mobilization, hydration, sensory aids)
Bed rest with side rails and restraints to prevent wandering

questions.explanation: Delirium prevention in older adults is built on multicomponent non-pharmacologic measures: orientation with visible clocks and calendars, cognitive stimulation and family involvement, sleep enhancement, early and safe mobilization, adequate nutrition and hydration, correction of sensory deficits with glasses and hearing aids, and prompt removal of catheters. Pooled trial data show that such multicomponent interventions probably reduce the incidence of delirium compared with usual care.

optionExplanations.a: Optimal prescribing means avoiding precipitating medications including antipsychotics; evidence does not support routine antipsychotics for delirium management.
optionExplanations.b: Sedatives should be avoided as they are recognized precipitants; sleep aids are specifically discouraged as part of sleep enhancement.
optionExplanations.d: Diphenhydramine is an anticholinergic sedating antihistamine, exactly the class that should be avoided to prevent delirium.
optionExplanations.e: Restraints and immobility are counterproductive; early safe mobilization and removal of restraints are recommended.

source.reference: GM6 — Delirium Prevention in Older Adults

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman has fallen twice in 3 mo, both times at night while walking to the bathroom. She takes lorazepam 1 mg nightly for insomnia. Orthostatic blood pressures are normal, her gait is slow but steady with a properly fitted cane, her vision has been corrected, and a home hazard assessment has already been completed. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Gradual tapering and discontinuation of the lorazepam
Substitution of a different sedative-hypnotic at bedtime
Advising bed rest and restricted ambulation
Application of a night-time physical restraint
Prescription of a wheelchair for all mobility

questions.explanation: Fall interventions are directed at the identified intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors. Medication side effects and polypharmacy are extrinsic contributors, and taper or gradual discontinuation of psychotropic medication is a specific recommended intervention. With gait aid, vision, orthostatic vitals, and home hazards already addressed, her nightly benzodiazepine is the remaining modifiable risk factor.

optionExplanations.b: Swapping one sedative-hypnotic for another leaves the psychotropic exposure that contributes to falls in place.
optionExplanations.c: Immobility worsens deconditioning; muscle strengthening, balance retraining, and group exercise programs are recommended instead.
optionExplanations.d: Restraints are not a falls intervention and their removal is recommended in hospitalized older adults.
optionExplanations.e: A wheelchair for all mobility promotes immobility and does not address the medication-related risk; a fitted gait aid is already in place.

questions.question: An 80-year-old man has unintentionally lost 6 kg (about 5% of his body weight) over the past year. He reports feeling exhausted most days. His grip strength and his walking time over 15 feet both fall in the lowest 20% for his sex and body size, and his weekly energy expenditure is well below 383 kcal/wk. How should he be classified using the Fried physical frailty phenotype?

options.text: Frail only if cognitive impairment is also documented
Unclassifiable without a cumulative deficit frailty index

questions.explanation: The Fried physical frailty phenotype comprises five criteria: shrinking (unintentional loss of at least 10 lbs or 5% of body weight in the prior year), weakness (grip strength in the lowest 20%), poor endurance (self-reported exhaustion), slowness (walking time over 15 feet in the slowest 20%), and low activity (lowest 20% of kcal/wk). A patient is frail with 3 or more criteria and at-risk or pre-frail with 1 or 2. This man meets all five.

optionExplanations.a: Pre-frail applies to only 1 or 2 criteria; he meets all five.
optionExplanations.c: Meeting several phenotype criteria excludes a non-frail classification.
optionExplanations.d: Cognitive impairment is not one of the five Fried phenotype criteria.
optionExplanations.e: The cumulative deficit (Rockwood) frailty index is a separate model; the Fried phenotype can be applied on its own.

source.reference: GM9 — Models of Frailty: Physical Frailty Phenotype (Fried et al.)

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman describes involuntary loss of small amounts of urine when she coughs, laughs, or lifts her grandchild. She has no urgency or nocturia, denies dysuria, and mobilizes independently without cognitive impairment. Post-void residual is 20 mL, and urinalysis and urine culture are normal. Which of the following is the most likely type of incontinence?

options.text: Transient incontinence secondary to urinary tract infection

questions.explanation: Urinary incontinence is any involuntary loss of urine and has four subtypes: stress incontinence, which is leakage associated with physical strain; urge incontinence; overflow incontinence; and functional incontinence. Leakage triggered specifically by coughing, laughing, and lifting, with no urgency, a low post-void residual, and preserved mobility and cognition, is stress incontinence.

optionExplanations.a: Urge incontinence is leakage associated with an oversensitive bladder and a strong urge to urinate, which she denies.
optionExplanations.b: Overflow incontinence reflects poor bladder emptying; her post-void residual is normal at 20 mL.
optionExplanations.c: Functional incontinence is leakage due to illness or disability unrelated to the urinary tract, but she is independent and cognitively intact.
optionExplanations.e: Infection is a transient cause of incontinence, but her urinalysis and culture are normal and she has no dysuria.

questions.question: An 84-year-old bedbound man in long-term care has a sacral wound. On examination there is full-thickness loss of skin with visible adipose tissue, rolled wound edges, and a small amount of slough that does not obscure the base. No fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, or bone is visible or palpable. How should this pressure injury be staged?
questions.explanation: In the NPIAP staging system, stage 3 is full-thickness loss of skin with adipose tissue visible, where slough or eschar may be present and granulation tissue and epibole (rolled wound edges) are often seen. Because deeper structures are not exposed and the wound base can be assessed, this is stage 3.

optionExplanations.a: Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis and a viable pink or red moist wound bed, without visible adipose tissue.
optionExplanations.c: Stage 4 requires exposed or directly palpable fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage, or bone.
optionExplanations.d: An injury is unstageable only when slough or eschar obscures the extent of tissue damage; here the base is visible.
optionExplanations.e: Deep tissue pressure injury describes intact or non-intact skin with localized non-blanchable maroon or purple discolouration or a blood-filled blister.

source.reference: GM13 — Table 5. NPIAP Staging System for Pressure Injuries

questions.question: A 79-year-old man with dementia attends with his daughter, who reports that over the past year he has become unable to manage his finances or his medications independently, and last month he became lost driving to a familiar store. His MMSE is 22/30. He insists he is a safe driver and wants to keep his licence. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: He may continue driving and be re-evaluated in 6-12 mo
He may continue driving because his MMSE score is above 20
He may continue driving in daylight hours and on familiar routes only
He should stop driving, as inability to independently perform 2 or more IADLs indicates at least moderate dementia
He may continue driving while awaiting an on-road test at a specialized centre

questions.explanation: Moderate to severe dementia is a contraindication to driving, defined as the inability to independently perform 2 or more IADLs or any basic ADL. This man can no longer manage finances or medications, which are two IADLs, so he should be advised to stop driving. Physician reporting to the Ministry of Transportation is mandatory in all Canadian provinces and territories except Quebec, Nova Scotia, and Alberta, where it is discretionary.

optionExplanations.a: Assessment and re-evaluation every 6-12 mo applies to patients with mild dementia who are deemed fit to drive, not to moderate dementia.
optionExplanations.b: The MMSE score alone, whether normal or low, is insufficient to determine fitness to drive.
optionExplanations.c: Time-of-day or route restrictions are not offered as an alternative when moderate dementia contraindicates driving.
optionExplanations.e: Referral to a specialized driving centre is used for patients with mild dementia; it does not justify continued driving in moderate dementia.

source.reference: GM14 — Driving Competency / Table 6. Conditions That Impair Driving

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman was started on a drug for nausea. Weeks later she developed a resting tremor and rigidity, which were treated as new Parkinson's disease with levodopa. She then became orthostatic and was given fludrocortisone. She now takes 11 medications, and no one has questioned the original prescription. Which of the following best describes what has occurred?
questions.explanation: A prescribing cascade is the process whereby an adverse drug reaction is misinterpreted as a new medical condition and a further drug is prescribed to treat the drug-induced event. Prescribers should ask whether the new drug is being used to address an adverse effect of an earlier drug, whether the original drug is really needed, and whether its benefits outweigh the harms; avoiding treatment of an adverse drug reaction with another medication is a key way to prevent polypharmacy.

optionExplanations.a: Non-adherence refers to failure to take medications as prescribed, and compliance falls with increasing numbers of drugs; it does not describe this sequence.
optionExplanations.c: A drug-drug interaction is one drug altering the effect of another; here each new drug was added to treat the previous drug's adverse effect.
optionExplanations.d: Therapeutic duplication means two agents with the same action; these drugs have different indications.
optionExplanations.e: Tolerance is a reduced response to a drug over time and does not explain the sequential additions.

questions.question: A 79-year-old man who lives alone is brought by his daughter because of unintentional weight loss over the 6 mo prior to this visit. Since his wife died he has been forgetting meals and has dental problems. On examination his BMI is 21.0, with temporal wasting, muscle wasting, and loss of subcutaneous fat. He is afebrile with no localizing symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to search for occult malignancy
CBC, electrolytes, calcium/albumin, magnesium, phosphate, creatinine, LFTs, vitamin B12, folate, and TSH
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsy

questions.explanation: For unintentional weight loss and suspected malnutrition in an older adult, the source specifies an initial panel of CBC, electrolytes, Ca2+/albumin, Mg2+, PO4, creatinine, LFTs (INR, bilirubin), vitamin B12, folate, TSH, and lipid profile. His history of cognitive decline with forgetting meals, dental problems, and living alone are the listed functional and social contributors, and his BMI below 23.5 in a male together with temporal wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat are the physical findings that should raise concern. Broad imaging is not the described first step.

optionExplanations.a: Functional imaging is not among the investigations listed for malnutrition and weight loss in older adults.
optionExplanations.b: Cross-sectional imaging is not part of the described initial workup for unintentional weight loss; treatment is directed at underlying causes identified by assessment and baseline bloodwork.
optionExplanations.d: Endoscopy is not a first-line investigation here; referral described is to a speech language pathologist for swallowing assessment and to a nutritionist.
optionExplanations.e: Urinalysis, ESR, and CXR are described as investigations to consider only if indicated by the assessment, not as the initial panel.

source.reference: GM12 — Malnutrition and Weight Loss: Clinical Features, Investigations, and Treatment

questions.question: An 84-year-old woman with dementia in a long-term care home has been passing loose stool frequently for 5 d. She is immobile and takes opioids for osteoarthritis pain. For months she has had <3 bowel movements per wk with straining, hard stools, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation. She is afebrile and rectal examination reveals hard stool in the rectum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In older adults, chronic constipation may present as fecal impaction and over flow diarrhea, which is the pattern of hard stool in the rectum with loose stool escaping around it. Opioids, anticholinergics, immobility and non-optimal positioning, and dementia are all listed etiologies of constipation, and straining, hard stools, sensation of incomplete evacuation, and <3 bowel movements per wk satisfy the Rome IV diagnostic criteria. Alarm symptoms such as fever, hematochezia, or severe abdominal pain are absent.

optionExplanations.a: Fever is listed as an alarm symptom prompting a different work-up; she is afebrile and has hard stool palpable in the rectum, which points to impaction.
optionExplanations.c: The diagnosis of chronic constipation requires that the patient not meet Rome IV criteria for IBS, and her picture is impaction with overflow rather than a functional bowel disorder.
optionExplanations.d: Her longstanding pattern is constipation with hard stools rather than laxative excess, and chronic laxative use is something the source discourages rather than the explanation for this presentation.
optionExplanations.e: Hematochezia, severe abdominal pain, and acute onset would be the alarm features suggesting another colonic diagnosis; none are present.

source.reference: GM4 — Presentations in Older Adults: Constipation

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman living in her own home in Ontario attends clinic with her grown son, on whom she relies for bathing, shopping, and banking. She is withdrawn with poor eye contact, appears malnourished, and has unexplained bruises. When the son leaves the room she says he has threatened her and used her money against her will. She is alert and gives a coherent history. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange urgent placement in a long-term care home to separate her from her son
Report the suspected abuse to the provincial authority, since reporting is mandatory in Ontario for every older adult
Ask the son to answer the Elder Abuse Suspicion Index questions on her behalf
Assess her decision-making capacity regarding any proposed intervention and address imminent safety
Defer any intervention until the bruises are documented by a second clinician at a follow-up visit

questions.explanation: Management of suspected elder abuse begins with assessing the patient's decision-making capacity regarding any proposed intervention and addressing imminent safety, then referral to local resources, creating an emergency safety plan, and offering assistance with reporting abuse. Her presentation combines the listed victim characteristics of physical or emotional dependence on a caregiver with the findings of withdrawn nature, poor eye contact, malnourishment, and bruises, and the perpetrator here is her grown child, the most common relationship in police-reported family violence against seniors.

optionExplanations.b: In Ontario, reporting elder abuse is mandatory when the older adult resides in a Long-term Care Home or a Retirement Home; she lives in her own home, so reporting is offered as assistance rather than imposed.
optionExplanations.c: Questions 1 to 5 of the Elder Abuse Suspicion Index are asked of the patient and question 6 is answered by the doctor, so the possible perpetrator is not the respondent.
optionExplanations.a: Institutional placement is not the described response; the listed options are home care, respite agencies, shelters, legal, police, and government-supported elder abuse consultants, chosen with the patient.
optionExplanations.e: Delaying while imminent safety is unaddressed conflicts with the stated management sequence of addressing safety and creating an emergency safety plan.

source.reference: GM7 — Elder Abuse: Risk Factors, Screening Tools, and Management

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman living at home reports involuntary discharge of stool without awareness, three to four times per week for the past month. Six weeks ago she was started on a laxative. She is cognitively intact and independently mobile. Digital rectal examination shows an empty rectal vault, normal resting tone, and a normal anal squeeze. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Start an antimotility agent such as loperamide
Refer for biofeedback and retraining of the pelvic floor muscles
Perform disimpaction and start a program to prevent impaction
Refer for direct surgical repair of the anal sphincter

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists medication (e.g. laxative, anticholinergics, antidepressants, caffeine, muscle relaxants) among the causes of fecal incontinence, and the management of medication-related causes is to stop laxatives, lower the dose, or discontinue any other offending agent. Her passive incontinence - involuntary discharge of stool without awareness - began after a laxative was started, and an empty rectal vault with normal resting tone and anal squeeze argues against fecal impaction and against sphincter weakness. Withdrawing the offending laxative is therefore the best initial treatment.

optionExplanations.b: Antimotility agents such as loperamide are directed at incontinence from physiological changes with age and loose stool, not at incontinence that a reversible offending drug fully explains.
optionExplanations.c: Biofeedback and retraining of pelvic floor muscles address weakened anal squeeze from age-related change or neurogenic causes; her resting tone and anal squeeze are normal.
optionExplanations.d: Disimpaction and impaction prevention are the management for incontinence caused by constipation or fecal impaction, but her rectal vault is empty.
optionExplanations.e: Direct surgical repair or augmentation of the sphincters is reserved for traumatic or iatrogenic sphincter injury, which she does not have.

questions.question: An 84-year-old woman with advanced dementia is medically stable and ready for discharge from hospital. She needs full assistance with all activities of daily living, is incontinent, and requires two-person transfers and nursing supervision through the night. Her husband is her only caregiver and can no longer manage at home despite maximal home and community support services. She is not terminally ill. What is the most appropriate discharge destination?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies residential healthcare institutions by the level and type of support the patient requires. A long-term care/skilled nursing facility provides around the clock nursing care and on-call physician coverage, and often offers occupational therapy, physiotherapy, respiratory therapy, and rehabilitation services. This woman needs full assistance with all ADLs plus nursing supervision overnight, which exceeds the minimal to moderate assistance the other residential options are designed for, and she is not terminally ill.

optionExplanations.a: Older adults affordable housing is for seniors who live independently and manage their own care but prefer to live near other older adults; rent is adjusted based on income and no personal care is provided.
optionExplanations.b: Retirement home residents are fairly independent and require only minimal support with ADLs and IADLs, far less than this patient needs.
optionExplanations.c: Supportive housing is for residents who require minimal to moderate assistance with daily activities while still living independently, usually in a rental apartment unit.
optionExplanations.e: Hospice is for terminally ill patients and their families, focusing on quality of life, and often requires a prognosis of 3 mo or less; she is not terminally ill.

questions.topic: Levels of Care and Healthcare Institutions
